extracted.intended_audience: criminalists, judges, forensic investigators, and legal psychologists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for criminalists on judging character, testimony, and the reliability of witnesses/defendants by observing behavior, habit, health, intelligence, and short-term changes. Emphasizes factual observation, repeated examination, and avoidance of personal bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference from vocation and life-circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the fundamental inclination of the person by considering his calling, his way of approaching his work, his environment, his choice of a wife, his preferred pleasures, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use occupation, working habits, environment, relationships, and preferences as evidence of underlying inclination and connect that inclination with the deed in question; base inferences on observed facts rather than labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on observable facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The emphasis must be on the fact; what is factual may be discovered, and these discoveries may be of use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground judgments in discoverable factual evidence (behavior, statements, corroboration). Avoid speculative typologies that lack factual support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying on ancient temperament categories
rubrics_metrics.description: The ancient classification of individuals according to temperaments is of little use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rigidly apply humoral/temperament labels; if using temperament language, stick to its significant general meaning (e.g., 'cautious' or 'reflective') rather than fixed categories, because temperament changes with age, health, and experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as diagnostic evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: If in the theater, you know the subject of laughter, the manner of laughter, and the point at which laughter first occurred, you know where the most educated and the least educated people are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe the subject, manner, timing, and cessation of laughter: embarrassed snickering, painful smiles, cruel laughter, happy/weak laughter, etc., can indicate education, guilt, cruelty, innocence, or malice. Concealment during laughter is difficult—laughter can be highly valuable in determining a case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe short-term changes and use repeated examinations
rubrics_metrics.description: The criminalist who does not frequently see and deal with his subjects does not perform his duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent and later examinations often yield more accurate notions of motives and character than initial interviews; imprisonment and time can reveal or alter a person's behavior—therefore reassess subjects over time while guarding against contamination by prison-mates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider effects of imprisonment and bodily condition
rubrics_metrics.description: The bodily condition and the health of the prisoner change almost always... The influence of such effects on the mind is familiar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for changes in physique, health, and mental state due to imprisonment (or its absence). Recognize that confinement can produce embitterment, softness, delirium, or transient improvements in health that affect testimony and confessions; evaluate such evidence in light of medical/expert advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against the pathetic fallacy (investigator's projection)
rubrics_metrics.description: The commission of the pathetic fallacy is the judge’s greatest danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that an investigator's or judge's own culture, character, and what they themselves would do can bias interpretation; avoid inferring motives or facts solely because one would have acted similarly under the circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate stupidity with lack of intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Foolishness is an isolated property. It is not related to intelligence as cold to warmth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that stupidity (narrowness, egoistic viewpoint) can coexist with forms of intelligence; a person may be clever in one domain and foolish in another. Evaluate specific faculties rather than assuming a single intelligence–stupidity continuum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default assumption: treat interlocutor as roughly your own intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a great mistake to suppose the criminal more foolish than oneself... it is best to believe him to be just as intelligent as oneself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Until you have definite knowledge of a person's capacity, assume they are about as intelligent as you are. This avoids underestimating or oversimplifying motives and prevents systematic error in interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess practical wisdom by sacrifice-of-immediate-advantage test
rubrics_metrics.description: To be wise is to be able to sacrifice an immediate petty advantage to a later and greater advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the pragmatic criterion—willingness to forego immediate petty gains for greater later gains—to evaluate whether a person acted with prudence/wisdom; apply this test when estimating the probability of someone's participation in calculated crimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat transient increases of mental activity cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: Very foolish people--idiots and lunatics--either because of anxiety, terror, wounds in the head, or shortly before death, become intelligent for a brief period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that acute stress, injury, or pathological states may temporarily increase apparent lucidity; testimony or statements made under such transient states have diminished reliability and should be corroborated and weighed with expert input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate persons by exceptional acts, not only habitual demeanor
rubrics_metrics.description: We must not take man to be what he seems most of the time, but what he shows himself as, in exceptional cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For forensic purposes, emphasize the subject's behavior in exceptional or relevant circumstances (the immediate self-expression related to the deed) rather than assuming everyday comportment fully characterizes culpability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertain and test claimed habits
rubrics_metrics.description: We have... to know whether and how far the witness behaved according to his habits. For by means of this knowledge we may be able to see the likelihood of many a thing that might have otherwise seemed improbable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate assertions that actions were habitual because demonstrable habit makes improbable events plausible (e.g., habitual spitting out a window explaining why someone was at that window). Seek corroboration, demonstrations, or third-party confirmation where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish habit from skill and habituation
rubrics_metrics.description: Habit makes actions easy. Habituation makes them necessary... skill is possible only where habit exists, and habit is present where a certain amount of skill has been attained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate whether a behavior is automatic (habit) or skilled (trained ability). Understand that habit may operate without conscious thought and can produce conduct the subject cannot readily explain—test claims empirically when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize difficulty of establishing private habits
rubrics_metrics.description: They occur mainly in isolated people--old bachelors and old maids--so that their confirmation by others is rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious when accepting habit-based explanations for solitary individuals; corroboration may be scarce, so seek indirect evidence and weigh habit-claims accordingly.
